 3. The Case of the Respondents: 

 The Rule was opposed on behalf of the respondents by swearing an affidavit-in-opposition on 9-12-2003 denying all material allegations. It is stated in the said affidavit-in-opposition, in reply to the statements made in paragraph 8 of the petition, that the background on which the petitioner was promoted to the rank of Air Marshal, is not known to the Air Head Quarters, that the complications were caused due to improper filling up of his pension papers for which it took a long time to make it ready, that the pension case of the petitioner had not been baulked at anywhere for no fault of the respondents. It is further stated at paragraph 11 of the affidavit-in-opposition that after clearing of the audit objection a charge-sheet was submitted against him in a corruption case involving purchase of Mig-29 aircrafts. This case resulted in the non- settlement of his pension benefit which cannot be done till he is acquitted from the said case (Annexure 6). It is however, explained that because of the pending criminal case he could not be placed in any category entitling him for ration facilities. It is further stated at para 26 that the grant of pension does not solely depend on BAF authorities but is wholly connected with his involvement in the said criminal case. It is further stated in paragraph 27 of the affidavit-in-opposition that the sanction of pension is a long drawn process and requires a lot of papers, that there are as many as 21 varying stages in the pension table for settlement of a pension case but the petitioner had so far crossed 8 stages and now it is stuck up for his involvement in the criminal case because grant of pension is subject to further good conduct and not otherwise. 

 4. Further case of the Parties:  An affidavit-in-reply on behalf of the petitioner was sworn on 4-4-2004. It is stated that, inter alia, therein that the petitioner was never involved in any case of corruption and that his pension was being held up for the last one year and ten months merely on flimsy grounds. 

 5. A supplementary affidavit was also filed on behalf of the respondents sworn on 18-5-2003. It is stated therein that it took 7 (seven) years to settle the pension case of Air Vice Marshal Mumtazuddin Ahmed and the pension case of Air Vice Marshal Altaf Hossain Chowdhury could be settled in a short period because he surrendered his LPR. It is further stated therein that since the pension case of the petitioner has not yet been finalised and is still pending before the authorities, the writ petition itself is premature and the Rule is liable to be discharged. 

 Mr AFM Mesbahuddin, thelearned Advocate appearing on behalf of the petitioner, submits that the petitioner joined the Air Force of former Pakistan as a GD Pilot in 1966 and had a brilliant record as an Officer both in Pakistan Air Force as well as in Bangladesh Air Force. He maintained an unblemished career with no stigma throughout his long career and he maintained the highest degree of professionalism in the Air Force which will be apparent from the letter dated 7-6-2001, but long after his retirement, when his papers in connection with his claim of pension was being made ready, a false case has been instituted in connection with the purchase of Mig-29 Fighter Planes. The learned Advocate further submits that the decision to purchase the said squadron of the fighter planes was taken by the highest level of the Government in the greater interest of the country and there was no iota of any corruption of criminality in making such a purchase, that the Government in its wisdom and discretion decided to purchase such modern planes and he being the Chief of the Air Force at the relevant time, did his part in good faith to the best of his professional ability in due discharge of his duties as the Air Chief, as such, the said case was filed with false allegation only in order to harass and humiliate the petitioner and others. The learned Advocate further submits that the petitioner after his retirement is entitled to his pension benefit which had already been accrued to him because of his long, successful and unblemished career without any stigma whatsoever. The learned Advocate further submits that the-said criminal case is now under challenge before another Bench of this Court under section 561 A of the Code of Criminal Procedure. Under such circumstance, since the petitioner maintained an unblemished career all through without any allegations during the whole 36 (thirty-six) years of his service career and since the pension had already been accrued to him, he submits, the Government is obliged to settle his pension benefits without further delay. 

 On the other hand, Mr Karuna Moy Chakma, the learned Assistant Attorney-General, raises serious objections to the claim of settlement of pension in favour of the petitioner. His objection is based inter alia that the writ petition itself is misconceived, because the petitioner being a member of a disciplined force of Bangladesh, is not entitled to maintain a petition under Article 102 of the Constitution. In this connection, the learned Advocate relies on the decisions of Col. Md Hashmat Ali (Retd) of Bangladesh Army Medical corps vs Bangladesh reported in 47 DLR (AD) 1. Lieutenant General Abu Saleh Mohammad Nasim (Retd) vs Bangladesh 1998 BLD (AD) 251 = 51 DLR (AD) 101. Major General Moinul Hossain Chowdhury vs Government of Bangladesh and others 4 BLC (AD) 257. Secondly, since a judicial proceeding is pending against the petitioner, under section 10 of the Public Servants Retirement Act of 1974, the petitioner is not entitled to get any pension benefit till the disposal of the said proceedings. The third ground raised on behalf of the respondents is that the grant of pension is dependent on rule 3 and rule 5 of Companies of Military Pension, 1981 (the Pension Regulation). He submits that if the service of the incumbent is not found satisfactory, the competent authority, under rule 3, may withhold his pension benefits. Besides, he submits, under rule 5, grant of pension is subject to future good conduct also and may be withheld or held in abeyance and in this case, since the petitioner had been involved in a criminal case which signifies anything but good conduct on his part, his pension case could not be settled. In this connection, he referred to the letter dated 7-5-2003 (Annexure-6) under the signature of Deputy Controller General, Defence Finance, stating that since a charge-sheet had been submitted against the petitioner, the grant of pension would not be proper till he is acquitted. 

 We have heard the learned Advocates of both the sides and went through the petition, the affidavit-in-opposition the affidavit-in-reply, the supplementary affidavits, filed on behalf of both the parties. There is no doubt that the petitioner was a brilliant officer and had a successful career both in Pakistan Air Force as well as in Bangladesh Air Force and ultimately rose to be the highest officer in the Air Force and retired with the rank and status of an Air Marshal. There is no allegation of misconduct against him during his long career. It is also understood that the pension of the petitioner has been withheld because of the pendency of a criminal case in which a charge-sheet had already been submitted against him and others. 

 12. On the basis of the above noted decisions, the learned Assistant Attorney-General submits that the petitioner being a retired member of the Air Force, a disciplined force of Bangladesh, he cannot at all maintain an application under Article 102 of the Constitution, as such, this writ petition itself is misconceived and is liable to be discharged. But such submission of the learned Assistant Attorney- General is too sweeping, not correct and is itself misconceived. 

 22. It is true that the framers of the Constitution, in their wisdom, limited the Constitutional protections only to the civil servants and purposely refrained from extending similar constitutional protections to the members of the defence services because of their special functions and rigorous duties but in spite of such limitation of protection a Court of law would not be slow to allow appropriate relief in a proper case. 

 24. In the case of Major (Retd) AFM Hajizur Rahman vs Government of Bangladesh 29 DLR 34, an order passed by the Chief of Staff, Bangladesh Army, cancelling the appointment of the petitioner as the officiating Judge Advocate General, was called in question under Article 102 of the Constitution. The Rule was discharged on the ground that the very subject of the petition relates to the terms and conditions of service and that the petitioner got no legal right to be enforced by this Court, but Shahabuddin Ahmed, J (as his Lordship then was), on the question of maintainability of the writ petition, held at para 5 : 

 "21 ....we hold that the petitioner got no legal right to be enforced by this Court. In other words, the petitioner got no cause of action. Absence of causes of action in a particular case should not be confused with the absence of the court's jurisdiction. Under Article 102 of the Constitution this court got jurisdiction to entertain application questioning the legality of any orders of Ministry Authorities other than a Court Martial, provided the orders are not in respect of conditions of service of military personnel.... 

 In the case of Rear Admiral AA Mustafa vs Bangladesh 51 DLR (AD) 147, the order of retirement of the petitioner was unsuccessfully challenged before the High Court Division and the appeal before the Appellate Division was also dismissed. While dismissing the petition or review, Mustafa Kamal CJ held at page 8:

Md Hashmat Ali (Retired) vs Government of Bangladesh 47 DLR (AD) 1 relied on by the learned Assistant Attorney-General the compulsory retirement of the petitioner was challenged under Article 102 of the Constitution. The High Court Division rejected the writ petition. The appeal was also dismissed by the Appellate Division. MH Rahman J (as his Lordship then was) held at para 16: 

 28. Besides, none of the conditions mentioned above applies to the grievance of the petitioner in the instant case. The petitioner here is praying for settling his accrued right to pension. He is not challenging any order of a Court or tribunal, as such, this decision rather, helps the petitioner to maintain his petition. 

 29. In the case of Lieutenant General Abu Saleh Mohammad Nasim (Retired) vs Bangladesh 1998 BLD (AD) 251= 51 DLR (AD) 101 the order of dismissal of the petitioner and his subsequent premature (Compulsory) retirement was challenged before the High Court Division. The High Court Division dismissed the writ petition summarily on the ground of maintainability. In dismissing the appeal Mustafa Kamal, J (as his Lordship then was), explained the underlying reasons as to why the members of the defence services hold their service during pleasure of the President, held at para 6: 

 "....all military personnel, especially the post of Chief of Army Staff which is a position of trust, hold their posts during the pleasure of the President. In the case of the civilian employees the pleasure theory is curtailed by constitutional provisions but in the case of military personnel there is absolutely no exception to the theory of pleasure of the President in the Constitution..." 

 30. This is a case of compulsory retirement involving tens and conditions of service of the appellant, as such, on the facts, this decision has got no manner of application so far the petitioner is concerned. This decision, although, highlights the concept of pleasure of the President but did not hold that the members of the defence services are totally disentitled to avail the constitutional remedies. 

 31. In the case of Major General Moinul Hossain Chowdhury vs Government of Bangladesh 4 BLC (AD) 257, the supersession of the petitioner was challenged under Article 102 of the Constitution. The High Court Division summarily rejected the said petition. The appeal before the Appellate Division was also dismissed. Latifur Rahman J (as his Lordships then was), held at para 7: 

 "...the post of Chief of Army Staff is it post in which the Government must have absolute trust, faith and confidence for the necessity of State security and naturally such a person in the post of Chief of Army Staff of a country holds office during the pleasure of the President as contemplated in Article 134 of our Constitution. Since the petitioner is a military personnel the doctrine of pleasure theory of the President as contemplated in the Constitution is applicable in this case, .contrary to Article 135 of the Constitution. For the foregoing reason, the petition filed under Article 102 of the Constitution is not maintainable. Apart from this, we do not also find any violation of the Army Regulations, 1960." 

 32. This is also a case on promotion involving terms and conditions of service, as such, on the facts this decision has got no manner of application so far the petitioner is concerned. 

 33. The correct legal approach, where a member of a defence service felt aggrieved by an action of the authorities, has been aptly explained by the Supreme Court of India in the case of Union of lndia vs Harjeet Singh Sandhu AIR 2001 SC 1772 RC Lahoti, J held at para 41: 

 "Exercise of power under section 19 read with Rule 14 is open to judicial review on well settled parameters of administrative law governing judicial review of administrative action such as when the exercise of power is shown to have been vitiated by malafide or is found to be based wholly on extraneous and/or irrelevant grounds or is found to be a clear case of colourable exercise of/or abuse of power or what is sometimes called fraud on power. i.e. where the power is exercised for achieving an oblique end The truth or correctness or the adequacy of the material available before the authority exercising the power cannot be revalued or weighed by the Court while exercising power of judicial review. Even if some of the material, on which the action is taken, is found to be irrelevant, the Court would still not interfere so long as there is some relevant material available on which the action can be sustained. The Court would presume the validity of the exercise of power but shall not hesitate to interfere if the invalidity or unconstitutionality is clearly demonstrated. If two views are possible, the Court shall not interfere by substituting its own satisfaction or opinion for the satisfaction or opinion of the authority exercising the power. 

 34. In the case before us, however, since no decision of a Court or Tribunal has been challenged nor an order affecting his terms and conditions of service has been questioned nor application of any disciplinary law has been raised on the principle settled in the case of Col. Md Hashmat Ali, this petition under Article 102 of the Constitution is maintainable. 

 36. In the instant case, the petitioner, an Air Force Officer, rose to become the Chief of Staff of Bangladesh Air Force and after attaining the age of superannuation, retired from the active service on 4-6-2001. There is no allegation of any misconduct during his long career but after his retirement, a case of corruption involving purchase of a squadron of Mig-29 fighter planes was instituted. After investigation a charge-sheet was also submitted against the petitioner and others. 

 "10. Public Servants not entitled to retirement benefits in certain cases. If any judicial proceedings instituted by the Government or, as the case may be, employer or any departmental proceedings are pending against a public servant at the time of his retirement or as the case may be ceasing to be in service he shall not be entitled to any pension or other retirement benefits except his subscriptions to any provident fund and the interest thereon till the determination of such proceedings and the payment to him of any pension or other retirement benefits shall be subject to the findings in such proceedings, 

 38. On a plain reading of the above provision. it would appear that in order to bring a public servant within the mischief of section 10, the Government has to show that a judicial proceeding or a departmental proceeding was pending at the time of his retirement but subsequent proceeding long after the retirement of a public servant would not come within the ambit of section 10. 

 39. In the instant case, there was no allegation of any judicial proceeding or departmental proceeding pending against the petitioner at the time of his retirement on the completion of his age of superannuation on 4-6-2001, as such, he does not come within the mischief of section 10 of Act XII of 1974, 

 The next ground urged by the learned Assistant Attorney-General is that under rule 5 of the Compendium of Military Pension, 1981, the grant of pension is subject to future good conduct and the concerned authority may withhold such pension of the incumbent in case of any incident or allegation which is contrary to his good conduct, that since in the instant case, a charge-sheet has already been submitted against the petitioner in a case of corruption which signifies anything but good conduct on the part of the petitioner, the pension and other benefits are justifiably withheld till he is acquitted from the said criminal case. 

 (b) In special circumstances to be determined by the Government of Bangladesh the pension (service, disability or family), children's allowance or gratuity granted to an individual under this Regulation or any portion of it, may be suspended or withheld. In exceptional cases, payment of part or the whole of the pension, allowance or gratuity suspended may, by order of the Government of Bangladesh, be made to the wife or other dependents of the pensioner." 

 47. A person may be an accused in a criminal case but unless he is found guilty by a Court of law he is deemed to be innocent in the eye of law. He will face the trial as an innocent man as anybody else. It is always for the prosecution to prove beyond reasonable doubt that he is guilty of the offence as charged. No disability can touch him till he is found guilty on evidence by a Court of competent jurisdiction. This is a settled and fundamental principle in Criminal Jurisprudence and accepted in all canons of law all over the globe. 

 48. In the instant case, although charge-sheet has been filed against the petitioner but till he is found guilty by a Court of law, he will be deemed to be innocent and his conduct would also deemed to be and continue to be good unless and until he is convicted.

 52. As such, it is apparent that neither rule 3 nor rule 5 has got any manner of application in the facts and circumstances of this case entitling the respondents to withhold the pension and other retirement benefits of the petitioner.
